## Step 1: Examine reads

Reads are linked into `raw_data/`.
```{r}
#cd ~/mb5370-workshops/raw_data

## symbolic link to rae reads file in the raw_data folder 

#ls -l raw_data
## using ls to make sure the link is correct for the raw data 

#zcat raw_data/raw_reads.fastq.gz | head -n 40000 | bioawk -c fastx '{print $name,length($seq)}' > read_lengths.txt

#lines underneath explain the code 
# Unzips the raw data and sends the data to standard output
##zcat raw_data/raw_reads.fastq.gz \
# This is a pipe. It sends output from the previous command as input to the next command
  ##| \
# Here we select only the top 40k lines in the file. This equates to 10k reads. It should be plenty to get some stats
 ## head -n 40000 | \
# This is a small bioawk program. It prints the name of each sequence followed by its length
  ##bioawk -c fastx '{print $name,length($seq)}' \
# Send outputs to a file called read_lengths.txt
##  > read_lengths.txt

#making a graph to visualise the data 
library(tidyverse)

rl_data <- read_tsv("read_lengths.txt",col_names = c("id","length"), show_col_types = FALSE)

ggplot(rl_data, aes(x=length/1000)) + 
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2) +
  xlab("Read Length Kb") + ylab("Number of Reads")

#Figure 1: Histogram of read lengths in the mock nanopore sequencing dataset

# calculating read N50 
total_len <- sum(rl_data$length)

rl_data |> 
  arrange(desc(length)) |> 
  mutate(cumsum = cumsum(length)) |> 
  filter(cumsum>total_len/2) |> 
  head(n=1)



```

## Step 2: Assembly

Commands run in `flye_metagenome/`.

```{r}
#Step 2
#running the batch file 
#sbatch run_flye.sh 
#tail -f slurm-XXX.out to monitor job output 
#it took 
#3.1 - 
#creating a plain text and pasting this - to calculate GC content and size 
# Bioawk script for calculating gc and printing name,length,GC
BEGIN {
    OFS="\t"
}

{
    l=length($seq)
    ngc=gsub("[cgCG]","",$seq)
    nat=gsub("[taTA]","",$seq)
    print $name,l,ngc/(ngc+nat)
}

#saving as gc.awk
```
